I'll need to find it again, as I don't remember if it was a reddit thing or a tiktok thing. But it made a compelling argument that Cleric's are closer to sugar babies and Warlocks are actually the ones with a stricter patron.
paladins are the sweet spot
considering that the cleric capstone is successful divine intervention vs the warlock capstone of being able to ask for all your spell slots back
Cleric and Warlock. One calls their Daddy, the other calls Father. It's just different than what you expected.
I almost always dm the cleric's god as distant, but the pact keeper as mettlesome

in the case of cleric vs celestial warlock, i always play it like the cleric is an official representative and the warlock is the sleeper/secret agent the god sends out to do some below the table missions

so lorewise, warlocks dont get their power from entities that have the spark of divinity.... they get their powers from powerful beings that are trying to stockpile enough power to get the spark of divinity.

clerics get their power from entities with the spark of divinity, or concepts that have the spark of divinity (like the concept of life, or death in of itself has enough faith to have that power)

paladins use the oaths like a foci between them and the spark of divinity, not nessessairly following a god or even 'concept' but following oaths to such a degree that gods that appreciate their dedication often imbue them with righteousness.

Now this gets muddled with creatures that have the spark, but havent enough faith to fully ascend, as they might make pacts while also having clerics

(this incorporates not just 5e lore - which changed paladins a lot - but also past editions) but basically warlocks take a sliver of power from something like a fiend, or celestial or whatever, and then using that, they gain experience and grow that sliver.  on death that sliver which is much larger is returned, and the being that loaned it has the accumulated power added to their own.

once they have enough power to be on that cusp of divinity, they need faith more than power, and thus start doing miracles (or the equivalent depending on the nature of the being) to get followers.  once they have 500+ followers (in some eds it took 2k followers, but 500 was the minimum) they can start imbuing clerics, and generally stop making pacts.
so pact keepers need to interact to push warlocks to greater power levels.  gods generalyl dont
(also in 2e, if you took the head of a god on its own divine plane, you took that gods position, and followers, and became that god)
(also all beings with souls - so most creatures - have a spark of divinity, but when talknig godhood, it has to be more than the mote nearly everyone has)

Cleric:

•Lots of spells slots

if you are following the rest rules properly, a warlock will get nearly the same number of spells per day as a cleric... so clerics get a lot that refreshes daily, warlocks get a few that refresh many times daily.

otherwise thats a good mechanical breakdown of the two

like at 11th level a cleric has a total of 16 spell slots spread fairly evenly between 1 and 5, plus a 6th.

an 11th level warlock should get 9-12 5th level slots, plus a 6th level per day.... thats only a handful less than cleric
Not necessarily, short rests aren't particularly a mandatory thing. And compared to clerics versatility a Warlock may not have need or situation to use their slots.
you are supposed to have at least 3 short rests per long rest, and its suggested that 4 or 5 is better
its outlined in the DMG that that is what you are supposed to do

for balance reasons... all classes are balanced around 3-5 short rests per long rest.

also only one long rest per 24 hour period, meaning after a long rest, 16 hour should pass
in fact, vancian casters (wizard, cleric, druid) are only balanced vs fighter and rogue if you have that many rests.  long resting after every fight makes vancian casters really really OP

Most games I've experienced (player, viewer, or DM) tend closer to 1 short per long. Yes there's certainly downtime but a short rest is "nothing more strenuous than eating, drinking, reading, or tending to wounds." So may end up with a 3 hour short rest of relaxing at a tavern, or 3 "short rest" during a day of uneventful travel.

as i said "if you are following the rest rules properly"

the rest rules in the DMG 'suggest' outline what is supposed to happen.  just as anything else, you can omit things to fit your table, but that will cause imbalances and will give way to statements like 'clerics get tons of spell slots' when if you follow the rules,its not that many more.

nothing wrong with it, but i did put in the caveat about playing the game as printed.  Just as nat1's and nat20s on skill checks mean nothing special, many tables make them special.... but you then shouldnt say how OP acrobatics is, casue you have a 5% chance of jumping to the moon

So when a DM sees this.  So Hampstead has surgery as an option for some items (The heart and the Aberrant Amber are two examples)

So there is a risk of when you get surgery done, you just die (and then have to be rebuilt, just the way we like or Frankenstein's Monsters here).  So I wanted something similar to old school system shock, but simplified to use a d20 and adjusted for the stats that are more common in 5e, namely 5e is typically higher)

```If someone goes under the knife for serious surgery in Hampstead, They must roll a d20 to see if they survive the procedure.  The roll cannot be modified, nor can advantage or disadvantage be applied.  The number they must roll above (not equal to) is 21-[con score].  If they fail this roll, they die, and must be rebuilt as per  the Hampstead rules for being brought back.```
